explanations.explanation: Seir it is. Moses says, “…for many days we wandered around Mount Seir.” Many days circling one mountain. You know when you drive around the same block three times hunting for a parking spot? Same energy, but with sandals.

Sinai is a famous mountain, friend, so I see why it jumped out. But verse 1 doesn't name it. Moses says Israel wandered around Mount Seir. When a name is stuck in your head, it'll try to jump into every answer.

Carmel never shows up in this passage. Moses says that for many days they wandered around Mount Seir. Grabbing a mountain name from memory is like grabbing a cookie straight off the rack. It looks right, but it hasn't had time to settle. Seir is the one.

Yes. The LORD says, “They will be afraid of you, so you must be very careful.” The text doesn't say why they'll be afraid. I think a whole nation marching through your backyard would make anybody a little nervous.

Flip it around, friend. The LORD says the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir, “will be afraid of you.” So it's Esau's people who are nervous here. Then comes the instruction: “…you must be very careful.”

Careful is the word. The LORD says Esau's people will be afraid, "so you must be very careful." Right after that He adds, "Do not provoke them." Think of walking through a stranger's kitchen with a full tray of cookies. Slow steps, friend.
Bold sounds heroic, and I love the energy! But the LORD asks for the opposite. Esau's people will be afraid, so Israel must be very careful. A big entrance would be the last thing the moment needs.

Quick makes sense if you picture hurrying past. But the word the LORD uses is careful. Rushing through somebody's house is how a lamp gets knocked over. Israel is told to be very careful with Esau's people.

explanations.answer: God gave Mount Seir to Esau
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. He says, “…because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession.” So the land was already given before Israel ever showed up. Nobody can claim a spot that's already taken, friend.

An army never comes up in these verses. In fact, the LORD says Esau's people will be afraid of Israel. The reason He gives is a gift: “…because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession.” It's about what He gave, not who could win a fight.

The text doesn't say anything about Israel asking or not asking. The LORD's reason is simple: “…because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession.” Asking nicely wouldn't change a gift that's already been given. You can't ask for the last cookie on a plate that already belongs to someone else.

explanations.answer: They pay for it in silver
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, and I mean that literally. The LORD says, “You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink.” They go through Seir as customers. I like it, friend. It's a clean way to be a neighbor.

Taking is not what the LORD says. He says, “You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink.” Walking out of a store with a full cart and a wave isn't shopping. It's a whole different thing.

Free would be nice, I won't lie. But the LORD says Israel is to pay in silver. The words are, “You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink.” So nobody hands out free samples on this trip.
Nothing! Moses says, “The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing.” Forty years of that. I can't keep a cookie jar stocked for forty minutes, friend.

Water is a good guess for a desert, I get it. But Moses says they have lacked nothing, and "nothing" covers everything. The LORD has been with them these forty years. That one word is bigger than any single item on the list.
Rest is a sweet guess, friend. But Moses' word is bigger than rest. He says the LORD has been with them these forty years, and they have lacked nothing. Not one thing is left off that list.

It's the other way around, friend. Verse 8 says, “We turned away from the Arabah road, which comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab.” So Israel leaves that road and takes the Moab road. It's like seeing your exit and actually taking it.

That's the one. Moses says, “We turned away from the Arabah road, which comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab.” They don't stay on the Arabah road. They turn onto the road of the Wilderness of Moab.

Not this time, friend. The LORD tells Moses, “Do not harass the Moabites or provoke them to war.” Moab's people are descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5). So Israel is told to leave them alone, not drive them out.

That's right. The LORD says, “Do not harass the Moabites or provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land.” The Moabites are descendants of Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5). Driving them out is the opposite of what He says.

explanations.answer: God gave Ar to Lot's descendants
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The LORD says, “…because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.” Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5). Same kind of reason as with Esau's land, friend.

explanations.answer: Moab's cities are too far away
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't mentioned here at all. The LORD gives a different reason: “…because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.” It's not about how far the road is. It's about who the land was given to.

explanations.answer: Moses made a deal with Moab
explanations.explanation: The text mentions no deal. Moses is just passing along what the LORD says: “…because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.” The land belongs to Lot's descendants because of what He gave. No paperwork needed.

explanations.answer: What Israel did in its own land
explanations.explanation: Yes. The note says Esau's people drove out the Horites and settled in their place, “just as Israel did in the land that the LORD gave them as their possession.” So Moses holds up Israel's own story as the comparison. Moses tucks it into the middle of a travel report.
Egypt isn't in this note at all. The comparison in verse 12 is about Israel in the land the LORD gave them. Egypt is a whole other chapter of the story. The note keeps its eyes on Seir.

explanations.answer: What Moab did to the Ammonites
explanations.explanation: Moab and Ammon aren't compared in this note. Verse 12 is about Seir and the Horites, and it ends, “…just as Israel did in the land that the LORD gave them as their possession.” That's the comparison. Easy to blend the neighbors together, friend.

True, and I love this part. The LORD says, "Now arise and cross over the Brook of Zered," and Moses says, “So we crossed over the Brook of Zered.” Back at Kadesh, Israel was unwilling to go up (Deuteronomy 1:26). Now the command comes and they go.
Not this time, friend. Moses says, “So we crossed over the Brook of Zered.” After the LORD's command to arise and cross, they cross. No dragging feet in this verse.

Thirty-eight years! Moses says it took that long from Kadesh-barnea until they crossed the Brook of Zered. I thought my years in the junk drawer I got stuck in were long. Thirty-eight years is a lot of wandering.
Twelve is already a long stretch, friend. But verse 14 gives a bigger number: thirty-eight years. That's how long it took from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered. It's a big one.
Seven years would feel like a long time on a trip, I'll give you that. But Moses says thirty-eight. That's the time from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered. It's way more than seven.

That's what Moses says. The trip lasted “…until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.” I think this is a heavy verse, so let's take it plainly. The time was counted out until that moment.

No king or open gate shows up in these verses. Moses says the thirty-eight years lasted “…until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.” I think this one is a heavy part of the passage. The clock ran until that happened.

explanations.answer: The cloud lifted from the camp
explanations.explanation: A cloud isn't mentioned in this passage. The verse says the time lasted “…until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.” I think this part is heavy, and Moses says it plainly. That's the moment the thirty-eight years run up to.

True. The LORD says, “…do not harass them or provoke them, for I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites.” Another neighbor, and the same kind of instruction. Israel is to keep a respectful distance.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, “…do not harass them or provoke them, for I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites.” So Israel is told to leave Ammon alone. No harassing.
None! Zero! Not a crumb! The LORD says, “…I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites.” Then He adds, “I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession.”

Half would be like splitting a cookie down the middle, but this isn't a sharing situation. The LORD says He will not give Israel any of the land of the Ammonites. He has given it to the descendants of Lot.
Most is a big bite, friend! But the LORD doesn't offer any bite at all. He says, “…I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites.” The answer is none.

explanations.answer: Drove them out and settled there
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 21 says the LORD destroyed the Zamzummites from before the Ammonites, “…who drove them out and settled in their place…” So the Ammonites took the land and made a home there. It's the same pattern the note gives for Seir.

explanations.answer: Left the land to the Moabites
explanations.explanation: The Moabites don't get that land in this verse. The Ammonites are the ones the text names, “…who drove them out and settled in their place…” Neighbors can be easy to mix up, friend. This land is Ammon's.

explanations.answer: Built a wall around the land
explanations.explanation: No wall is mentioned in the text. What the Ammonites do is “…drove them out and settled in their place…” They move in and stay. Nobody here is passing around a trowel.

Not quite, friend. Verse 22 says the LORD did for Esau's descendants what He did for the Ammonites, “…when He destroyed the Horites from before them.” So the LORD is part of the story there. I think it's easy to skip past a little note in parentheses.

That's right. The note says He did this for Esau's descendants who lived in Seir, “…when He destroyed the Horites from before them.” Then they drove them out and have lived there to this day. So the LORD's help is right there in the verse.
